speaker: Emily Heyward
title: EMILY HEYWARD: Build A Brand People Love (The Red Antler Way)
question: In brand strategy, why does testing candidate brand ideas with consumers often produce weak positioning?
guest: It's not easy, and I wish that I could give everyone an answer like, "Oh, then you test it, and you see which one wins." But I do not recommend that approach because unlike trying to determine a consumer insight, where research is incredibly valuable, if you're trying too heavily to rely on research to give you the answer, you're gonna land in a place that's very safe and predictable. People tend to be drawn to what's most familiar in a research setting versus what makes them uncomfortable and pushes things forward. So we use a number of criteria to evaluate our brand ideas. One is, does this feel true—does this actually connect to the experience this product or service delivers, and can we back it up? Two, does it feel differentiated? While you don't want to be so focused on your competition that you cede the territory every brand in your space needs to own, you still want to carve out a unique space. And three, the most important one, are people gonna care—does it actually answer this fundamental human need that this business exists to solve?

points.core: Consumer research excels at uncovering audience problems rather than choosing creative positioning.

points.core: Research participants instinctively favor familiar concepts over novel ideas that feel uncomfortable.
points.note: Accept: familiarity bias, status-quo preference, or test respondents rejecting unconventional ideas that push categories forward. Do not credit: generic clichés that customers do not know what they want.

points.core: Relying on consumer testing pushes brand strategy toward safe, predictable positioning.
points.note: Accept: convergence to generic category norms, watered-down messaging, or lowest-common-denominator concepts. Do not credit: vague complaints that testing is slow or expensive.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Consumer testing tends to reward the familiar and penalize the distinctive. When people evaluate brand ideas in a survey or focus group, they judge them rationally and out of context, so they gravitate toward concepts that are easy to understand, sound like what the category already says, and promise generic benefits everyone wants (quality, trust, value). Ideas that are genuinely new, polarizing, or emotionally charged score lower because unfamiliarity feels risky and people are poor at predicting what will actually move them in real life.

The result is regression to the mean: the "winning" idea is the least objectionable one, which is usually something competitors could claim equally well. Strong positioning requires sacrifice, meaning a choice to stand for something specific and appeal intensely to some people rather than mildly to all. Testing averages across respondents and so filters out exactly that edge.

There is also a structural problem: consumers can react to an idea, but they cannot weigh the company's capabilities, competitive whitespace, or long-term strategy. Positioning is a strategic decision, and outsourcing it to a popularity vote swaps judgment for consensus. Research is better used to inform and refine ideas than to pick them.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Testing candidate brand ideas with consumers often produces weak positioning because strong positioning requires sharp trade-offs, whereas consumer research systematically rewards familiarity and broad consensus. Effective positioning differentiates a brand by staking out a specific territory, which inevitably leaves some buyers indifferent or alienated. Concept tests and focus groups, however, average preferences across respondents, filtering out bold, polarizing ideas in favor of safe, lowest-common-denominator compromises. When asked to judge candidate ideas directly, people naturally gravitate toward reassuring category table stakes, such as quality, trust, or convenience, that sound appealing in isolation yet fail to separate a brand from rivals. Testing also puts respondents in an artificial, overly rational mindset, asking them to critique raw strategic concepts rather than experience finished creative execution amid real-world competitive clutter. Because genuinely distinctive ideas initially feel unfamiliar, early consumer feedback penalizes originality and steers brands toward generic, middle-of-the-road positioning that offends no one and compels no one.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Testing brand ideas with consumers tends to produce weak positioning because the method rewards what is familiar and safe. When people are shown abstract positioning statements, they judge them against what they already expect from the category. So they favor ideas that are clear, believable and pleasant, and those are usually the generic category benefits like quality, value, trust and convenience. Distinctive or provocative ideas can feel strange or polarizing at first, so they score worse, even though that edge is what would make the brand stand out.

Averaging across respondents makes this worse. The winning idea is often the least objectionable one, not the one a valuable segment would care about most. Bare concept statements also lack the creative execution, repetition and context that give an idea its power in the market.

Most fundamentally, positioning is a strategic choice about where the company can win against competitors given its real strengths, and consumers can't judge that. Research is useful for understanding what customers need and spotting confusion, but letting test scores pick the idea hands the decision to the people least able to make it.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Testing candidate brand ideas with consumers often produces weak positioning because research rewards what is immediately familiar and broadly acceptable rather than what is truly distinctive. When consumers evaluate abstract positioning concepts, they judge them against existing category norms. Conventional, safe ideas feel intuitive and score well, while bold or contrarian ideas—the very ones capable of carving out defensible space—often feel jarring, confusing, or overly narrow out of context.

Quantitative testing and focus groups also bias teams toward consensus, averaging away sharp edges to minimize negative reactions. Yet strong positioning is inherently exclusionary; it trades universal likeability for intense relevance to a specific audience. Furthermore, consumers react to the literal phrasing of a strategy statement rather than the full lived experience of the brand through product, design, and creative execution. As a result, relying on consumer validation to choose a brand direction systematically filters out originality and nudges brands toward generic, middle-of-the-road territory.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Consumer testing often produces weak positioning because it rewards ideas people understand and agree with immediately. Familiar claims tend to score well because they fit what people already expect from the category. Pick the idea with the highest average appeal, and you can end up with a promise that almost anyone likes and almost any competitor could make.

A positioning idea also gets judged differently as a sentence in a survey than it does when people encounter it through the product, advertising, and customer experience. A distinctive idea may need that context to make sense, and it may matter much more to the customers the brand most wants to win. Use research to find out who the idea resonates with, what they take it to mean, and whether they believe the brand can deliver it. The strategic choice is which relevant promise the brand can credibly make its own.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Consumer tests often ask which idea people like best. Strong positioning answers a different question: what should this brand stand for that gives its target customers a reason to choose it over competitors? A familiar promise can win broad approval precisely because people already expect it from every brand in the category. Meanwhile, an idea that resonates strongly with the intended audience can lose on average because it leaves other people cold.

Testing is most useful when it reveals what target customers take an idea to mean, whether they care about it, and whether they believe this particular brand can deliver it. Those findings inform the strategic choice. A popularity score alone can steer a brand toward a promise everyone agrees with and few people remember.
